title: Diving Deep into the Jhanas, with Leigh Brasington

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for modern mutants interested in mindfulness, meditation, awakening, states of high concentration, human sexuality, blockchain, science fiction, and much more. My name is Michael W. Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode I'm speaking with Leigh Brasington about practicing the jhanas. The jhanas refers to a Buddhist system of eight altered states of consciousness that arise during periods of high concentration. Leigh Brasington has been practicing meditation for decades and is the senior American student of the late venerable Ayya Khema. Leigh began assisting her in 1994 and began teaching retreats on his own in 1997. He teaches in Europe and North America and is the author of the book Right Concentration: A Practical Guide to the Jhanas. Find out more about Leigh's teaching and schedule at leighb.com. And now, without further ado, I give you the episode that I call Diving Deep into the Jhanas.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Hi Leigh, welcome to Deconstructing Yourself.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Thank you, it's very nice to be here.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, I was just thinking how nice it is to be able to actually do this in person, which I don't get to do that often.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, this is very excellent.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So Leigh, you are famous for teaching the jhanas, which in American meditation practice or Buddhist circles is sort of the inferior function.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: I'm not too worried about what the American faction is up to. I'm much more interested in what the Buddha had to say. After all, he was the guy we can be quite sure knew what he was talking about.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, due to the vagaries of history, and most American practice, especially in vipassana lineages these days coming through Ajahn Chah, there's a pretty strong de-emphasis on jhana, wouldn't you say?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Oh, yeah. In fact, we could take it not just to Ajahn Chah, who did practice the jhanas apparently — there's a lot of input from the Mahasi tradition. In fact, I would say that perhaps nationwide there's more Mahasi influence than Ajahn Chah influence. But the basic thing is that it's Theravadan influence. And Theravadan Buddhism is basically Visuddhimagga Buddhism. Now, the jhanas are a big part of what you find in the Visuddhimagga. But what you find in the Visuddhimagga are jhanas that are states so extremely concentrated, so extremely altered, that almost nobody can actually achieve these states. So it makes no sense to teach things that people can't do. So rather than exploring what possibly they can do for concentration, it seems it just got ignored.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That reminds me of the descriptions of practice that I hear from the Pa Auk Sayadaw folks.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, Pa Auk Sayadaw — I've actually sat with him. He's brilliant. If you want to learn Visuddhimagga Buddhism, he's the guy. Everything that he teaches is very firmly grounded in the Visuddhimagga, and his jhanas do seem to replicate what is described in the Visuddhimagga.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: If I'm not mistaken — and I'll just back up here for some listeners who don't know what we're talking about at all — jhana practice would be straight-up concentration practice rather than vipassana practice, which has more to do with deconstructing the sensory phenomena moment by moment. Would you agree with that short description?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. I would put it that concentration practice is generating indistractability, so you don't get lost when you're doing something, and then taking the indistractable mind and — vipassana practice — investigating what's actually happening.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes. So there's these, let's say, two wings of practice, or two directions of practice, and of course they reinforce each other and help each other. And Pa Auk Sayadaw is famous for being sort of the hardest of hard noses about what counts as real concentration. In his descriptions, you have to have not even a flutter of distraction in a continuous three-hour meditation for it to count as a, quote, real jhana. Correct?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: It seems, if you take all of the people teaching jhanas worldwide, that each one of them describes a system. And if you're doing their system, that's the real jhanas. And if you have more concentration than their system, you're indulging. And if you don't have as much concentration, of course it's not the real jhanas. And everybody agrees that their system is correct.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Strangely, they have the right one.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Why is there such a discrepancy about what counts as a real jhana, and furthermore, why does it have to have this seal of approval?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: I think part of the problem is that what we have is the Buddha's sermons, not his meditation instructions, for the most part. We get a little bit of meditation instruction, but it's a little bit. And what we have was preserved in an oral tradition for, let's say, approximately three and a half centuries.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, they did not write anything down for at least 300, 350 years. It was all just memorized in the heads of monks until many, many centuries later.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. And what happens in an oral tradition is that if you have a topic that gets discussed, then stock phrases are generated. And so you're now recounting one of the Buddha's sermons, and when you get to the jhana part, you just say the jhana stock phrase. So any variety in the Buddha's teachings, any details and so forth, all just begin to blend together into this basically one stock phrase for each of the jhanas. So the stock phrase is more of an indication that you should practice the jhana at this point, rather than how to practice the jhanas. In teaching jhanas, it's become quite apparent that written descriptions of them generally don't suffice. What's good is to give a description, either orally or written, and then have somebody go try out the instructions, and then have a one-on-one interview to sort of fine-tune it. So we didn't get the one-on-one interviews preserved. We just got the general description — not even the general instructions, but the general description. Given that we don't have a lot of detail, there is quite a lot of latitude of sort of trying to figure out, okay, what does this actually mean? And we wind up with literally probably more than a dozen descriptions of what the real jhanas are. And it basically varies on how much indistractability is associated with the states.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, there's a lot of different kinds of concentration, and there's an infinity of things one could concentrate upon. And knowing that the word jhana in Pali, or dhyana in Sanskrit, basically just means to concentrate or to meditate, why do we get this phrase that's so pointed, so specific — not “jhana, you're concentrated,” but “the jhanas”? Why are there the jhanas?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: I think primarily because of the stock phrase that shows up in the suttas — and this stock phrase appears more than a hundred times, it's quite frequent, and it appears always exactly the same. So it's obviously describing a specific state for each one of the jhanas. And so there is this specific state you're supposed to get into. So it is the jhana. Unfortunately, it's not really well delineated what exactly that state is, and so now we wind up with all these different interpretations.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So there are eight different applications, or eight different states, or eight different objects of concentration, that each qualifies as one of these eight jhanas.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. Although interestingly enough, in the suttas it's spoken of as four jhanas and four immaterial states. It's not until the Abhidhamma — so, say, 100 to 200 years after the Buddha — that we start finding the four immaterial states being called the four immaterial jhanas. Yes, there are these eight states that we now commonly refer to as the eight jhanas, and they are described over and over again in exactly the same way. So clearly there were eight states that were well known, well recognized, probably well delineated at the time of the Buddha. And we don't have much in the way of that delineation to figure out exactly what they were — although there are enough hints around to give us some pretty good ideas.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, the Buddha, of course, was not born a Buddhist. He was raised in the Vedic tradition, sort of pre-Hindu Hinduism. And he learned meditation not from Buddhists, but from these pre-Hindu Vedic teachers. Is it the case that he learned these jhanas and immaterial states from those teachers?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: We do have a sutta that indicates that he learned what we call the seventh jhana, the realm of nothingness or no-thingness, from his first teacher, and he learned the eighth jhana, the realm of neither perception nor non-perception, from his second teacher. It says nothing about the first four jhanas or the other two immaterial states. The assumption is that in order to learn seven and eight, he must have learned at least some of the preceding states. But we also have another description that indicates that he stumbled into the first jhana when he was probably an adolescent — so, say, a quarter of a century before his awakening.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So it's quite a beautiful moment. Yeah, by a river, under a tree.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, sitting under a rose-apple tree.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, it is quite a beautiful moment.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: And he recognizes this is a beautiful state, but apparently does nothing with it.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: And then we find, okay, he now knows jhanas seven and eight. Did somebody teach him the first four before he left home? Did he discover those on his own? I mean, we have no idea. He may have gotten the first seven from his first teacher. We just have no idea. We can speculate all we want. We do know that at the point he realized that his fasting almost to death wasn't going to work, he decided he had to do something else and began exploring the jhanas. So clearly he knew them by that point, but we don't have any hints as to how and when he learned them.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so he had learned these from other teachers. One is assuming, or I assume, that the jhanas then are important, and yet they're not the Buddha's unique contribution.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, correct. I would say his unique contribution is recognizing that when you have a well-concentrated mind, a post-jhanic mind, you now have a mind that can more accurately investigate reality. And that was the thing: concentrate your mind and then investigate what's actually happening. That was his real contribution.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And when we say “investigate what's actually happening,” that's what we would today call vipassana.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Correct.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, so we're going to use the concentration that we've gained in jhana practice to then closely examine our own sensory experience.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Correct. Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so how come almost nobody today does the jhanas and goes straight to vipassana?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Okay, well, as we discussed earlier, exactly what those states were is kind of difficult to ascertain. The names are quite unusual.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: So what happened, apparently, is that over time the states actually kept getting redefined. When you read what's in the suttas, it's very clear that one still has bodily awareness in the first four jhanas. And then as you begin reading the later material, starting with the Abhidhamma, you see — oh, concentration levels getting stronger, maybe not so much bodily awareness anymore. And then as you keep going through history until you reach the time of the Visuddhimagga — so we're talking 800, 900 years after the Buddha's death — there is no bodily awareness at all in any of the jhanas. So clearly things were changing.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: My best guess as to what was happening: okay, so the Buddha teaches these states and he leaves behind a sangha. These guys are out practicing in the wilderness. They got no TV, they got no women, got nothing to do but meditate.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: No smartphones.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: No smartphones, nothing like that. Whoever can do these states the deepest, that's the real jhanas. And there's a bunch of guys competing with each other to see who can get the most concentrated — more and more concentrated states, until we literally find in the Visuddhimagga it's saying that only one in a million, most optimistically, of those who come to meditation can get to the first jhana. It's actually in there. It's not phrased quite like that, but that's what it's saying. Whereas at the time of the Buddha, everybody was practicing jhanas. They didn't have a million followers.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So there was this sort of jhanic Olympics, or jhanic arms race, over many centuries, where people just got more and more intense about how focused you could possibly get.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Correct. That seems to be what's happening. It doesn't take much to examine the various descriptions over the centuries of literature and you see this quite clearly happening.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay, well, you know, I have pretty good concentration and I'm concentrating on a light switch right now. How is that a jhana or not a jhana?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: So the jhanas are described in ways that there are certain aspects of it that everybody agrees on. So the first jhana clearly has piti and sukha. We could translate piti as glee, although you see it translated as rapture, euphoria, ecstasy, delight. But I think glee maybe is the best translation.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Kind of giggly.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, it's got a giggly quality to it. And it's got a physical component. Sukha we could translate as happiness, joy. So if you're concentrated on something but you're not manifesting piti and sukha, then it's clearly not a jhana. Now, you could be concentrating and have piti and sukha occurring and it still not be a jhana. It appears that for it to become a jhana, what's necessary is that the object of your concentration becomes the experience of piti-sukha in the first jhana.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So it's not just being concentrated, but being concentrated on a specific object. So is it the case that you can have first-level jhana concentration on anything?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: No. First-level jhana concentration is concentrated on the experience of piti and sukha.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And that must be in your body.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Well, piti is going to manifest physically. It's going to have a physical component. Sukha, which is emotional — I mean, emotions do have bodily counterparts, so there's going to be somewhat of a counterpart there. The counterpart from sukha might just be a big grin. I certainly find when I'm in nice and deep and got nice, strong sukha, that's the physical counterpart to the emotion.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So what if I'm sitting here concentrating on this light switch, all rapturous and happy — is that a jhana or not?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Can you switch your attention from the light switch to the experience of piti and sukha and maintain the piti and sukha while you're focused upon it? If the answer is yes, then it's the first jhana.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Fascinating. So it does in the end come back to returning the attention to the piti-sukha. It must be in the body. That's interesting to me. And can you work it the other way around, where you intentionally generate piti-sukha and then focus on that?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yes, and in fact what I'm teaching, that's basically what I'm trying to get people to do. In order to generate sustainable piti and sukha, it's necessary to generate some degree of concentration. In the later commentaries, this basic level of concentration is called access concentration, because it gives you access to the jhanas.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Good idea.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: So you need to generate a certain degree of indistractability, and then the trick that I employed is that you switch from whatever object you were using to generate that indistractability to something pleasant, preferably a pleasant physical sensation. They seem to work better than mental sensations, because they tend to be more long-lasting and maybe don't have a story attached to them. Focus on that pleasantness to the exclusion of everything else. And if you do it well enough, it will set up a positive feedback loop of pleasure. Focusing on pleasure is pleasant. Focusing on pleasure pleasantly is more pleasant, right? So it throws in a little more pleasure. Oh, that's even more pleasant. All right, you've got the positive feedback loop, which generates the piti-sukha experience. Now shift your attention to the piti-sukha experience. Sustain the piti-sukha and your attention upon it. First jhana.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, if we were to make this term piti-sukha friendlier and talk about it in English, in two words or one word, what would you say to focus on?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Gleeful happiness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay. Joy in your body, something like that.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Something like that. Yeah, there's a lot of ways you can do it. And what's interesting in talking to hundreds of students that have experienced this — not everybody experiences it exactly the same way. There are degrees of intensity for both the piti and the sukha. So some people get a lot more rapturous experience, some people get a lot more joyous experience, some people it's just kind of mild for both, some people it blows the top of their head off.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And you brought up the idea of duration, and that is, in a way, the central point about concentration. Attention is where you want it to be — that's one part of concentration. But the other part is that it's there for as long as you want it to be there, or at least for a long time. So in the Leigh Brasington model, how long does attention need to be there to, quote, count?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Okay. So…

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I know this is the issue in the jhanas, right?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. So the word we translate as concentration is samadhi, and I think it's better translated as indistractability. So what does it mean to be indistractable? At access concentration, what I tell students is that you're fully with the object of meditation — your breath, the light switch, whatever it is — and if there are thoughts, they are wispy and in the background and don't pull you off into distraction. And you want to stay there for five to ten to fifteen minutes before switching from your initial object to the pleasant sensation.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So now, five to ten to fifteen minutes is pretty indefinite.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Some people, yeah, they get to access concentration and within a few seconds they can go into the first jhana if they know exactly what to do. Other people need to hang out there for quite a while. When you're first learning these states, it's going to be very helpful if you stay longer in access concentration before you switch to the pleasant sensation to try and trigger the first jhana. Once you get skilled at it, then maybe you stay for a little bit before you trigger it, knowing that you could have triggered it earlier, but the fact that you stayed longer will give you a deeper experience. So the answer to your question is, wow, it could be anywhere from a few seconds to several hours.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And why is this any better than, let's say, concentrating on a cloud or a rock or any other object? Why do we go into specifically meditating on this joyful happiness, or piti-sukha?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Because it works. I mean, that seems to be the thing. People that can access these states — and actually a lot of people do have the ability to access these states — moving through one, two, three, four, when they come out of the fourth jhana they have a mind that, well, as it says in the suttas, is concentrated, clear, sharp, bright, malleable, wieldy, and given to imperturbability. That is quite well suited for inclining and directing to investigating reality. So it seems that moving through these states has the advantage of upping the level of indistractability quite a bit over what you can generate by simply picking some object — the breath, the light switch, a candle, whatever — and just trying to stay with it. The breath or candle or even metta will get you to access concentration, but even coming out of a well-done first jhana you're going to be more indistractable than you would be coming out of access. And coming out of fourth jhana, it's actually quite remarkable how much more your mind will stay with whatever you want to focus on, and how little there is of anything else trying to impinge on your mind stream and drag you away.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So in other words, this specific sequence of concentration objects described as the jhanas is a great way to set up your vipassana practice.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay. But I notice you're stopping at the fourth jhana.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. It would appear from the suttas that the fourth jhana was sufficient. Getting to the higher jhanas is a more difficult task. I've had students who were quite good at the first four but never got beyond that, and yet were able to use the concentration from the first four jhanas to gain insight that was life-transforming. So I tend to sort of try and get people to four, and then have them start working with both doing their insight practice in the post-jhanic state of mind, and then sometimes working to see, okay, do they have sufficient concentration to get to the higher jhanas? It would appear that the higher jhanas do indeed give you more indistractability. I noticed quite a difference coming out of eighth jhana compared to coming out of fourth jhana, in terms of how quiet my mind is and how long it will stay in this really quiet space before it starts thinking about, well, whatever.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And the difference between the first four and the second four — the distinguishing factor, if I recall, is that the first four have concrete objects that you're focusing on, and the second four have abstract objects to focus on.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, that's a pretty good way of putting it. The first four have concrete emotions that you're focusing on. So the object is an emotion in each of the first four jhanas, with a bodily component, a bodily awareness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay, so you're aware of your body in each of the four.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: It's receding further and further into the background as the numbers go up.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, this is what's so fascinating to me, one of the many things. But the way I learned it emotionally — emotions are completely embodied. They may have thoughts that trigger them, or thoughts triggered by them, but the emotion itself is a bodily state. And so you would have to have body awareness to be in contact with it.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: The way I learned it, I would say that emotions are not totally bodily states.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: There is a mental aspect to them as well. And for me personally — and remember, I'm a thinking type as opposed to an emotional type…

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: You made your living as a coder.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, I was a computer programmer. I was basically a super coder.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, an old-school computer programmer.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. Yeah, I started out with coding pads, writing it in pencil.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: So yeah, for me, the focus in the first four jhanas is the mental aspect of the emotion, not so much the physical aspect. I'm very aware of the physical aspect in the background, but the foreground is the mental, emotional aspect.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, to me, when you say “mental aspect of an emotion,” that's almost impossible. So to me there would be thoughts about the feeling, or thoughts that are triggering the feeling. So what do you mean exactly?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Okay, it's not thoughts. It's the mental feeling.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So that's where I'm like, okay, it's a body sensation.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Well, okay. So not only am I a thinking type — from a perceptual standpoint, I'm visual and then auditory and very little kinesthetic.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So we're opposites.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly. So for me it's like, yeah, I can see the emotional, mental aspect, and that's what I focus on. It doesn't really matter, though. The whole idea is that you've got this piti-sukha experience, it's ongoing, and you can stay with it. Whether you call it mental or physical — well, that's just your concoction for trying to describe it, not your experience.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay, so we go to the mall, we grab a person and sit them down in a nice quiet place, and we say, we're going to teach you a jhana. How long does it take them to learn it?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Six months.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay. Of how much hard effort?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Okay, so first you've got to learn to meditate. Learning to meditate for some people comes quite naturally and they're pretty good at it right away. Other people, it takes quite a while. I would say that it took me about three years to get good enough so that I could start learning the jhanas. Now, three years — it wasn't three years of sitting every day and going to my group every week or anything like that. It was pretty sloppy. So if somebody were really into it, I would say that probably in six months of sitting every day, good instruction, a group that they can go to and get questions answered, do a couple of retreats in those six months — yeah, they'd be ready for jhana practice at that point.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I understand you teach the jhanas to a lot of people. I'm just curious — you know, we've got some interesting pushback in the mindfulness community, where some people seem to be not benefited that much by mindfulness. They have difficult breakdowns of certain sorts, or manifestations that are unpleasant. I'm curious, do you see that often, or even at all, when people are practicing jhanas?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yes. At the start of every retreat, I issue two warnings to people. The first warning is: if you have expectations, you're in big trouble. Expectations are the worst thing you can bring on any retreat. And if you have expectations of the jhanas, that's just going to get in the way. The second warning is that if you have any unresolved psychological stuff…

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Which none of us have.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly. Thankfully, we live in California. We got it all taken care of. If you have any unresolved psychological stuff, it may show up. And this happens whether you get to any jhanas or not. It's really a function, seemingly, of concentration. So the people who are practicing vipassana and who are getting into difficult psychological states — it's probably not as much the insights they're getting as the concentration they're generating while they're practicing vipassana.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: If you practice vipassana the way that's taught in the West, you're going to get some degree of concentration.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: You bet. And that can be enough to set you off. Normally you walk around and whatever that unresolved stuff is, you've got it well under control. You just keep it all pushed down. You start concentrating and, yeah, it can pop up. You don't have the energy to keep it pushed down anymore, because if you did, you wouldn't get concentrated.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So concentration can lead us into these difficult states. Why would we do it?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Because if you can handle the difficult state when it comes up, you can get it up and out, and it's no longer in there doing whatever it's doing behind the scenes and driving you nuts.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Right. So instead of being hidden away in the basement or the closet, you've, like, cleaned out the basement, cleaned out the closet.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Exactly. Exactly. You just need to have some support around, because when it comes up it could be — well, it could be pretty seriously bad.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Can you give me an example? One of the repeating themes in the podcast is informed consent, for people just to understand some of the stuff that arises.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Probably the most common thing that arises is some sort of feeling of unworthiness, some sort of low self-esteem.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: That seems to be our culture's baseline. That seems to be our culture's greatest failing.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah. Yeah. So it's not surprising that that's what shows up. You might have done some psychological work and you feel good about yourself on the surface, but now you get really quiet and whatever doubts were down there start to surface. Most psychological work seems to go in sort of a half-life form. In other words, you do some psychological work and you get half of that trauma or whatever taken care of, and you feel a lot better. But, you know, you get stressed again, and here comes up the remaining half, and you work on that, and you get half of that taken care of, and it just goes on like this. And there are enough adverse things that happen to people that, yeah, the half-life is always going to be there in the background, and it's going to pop up. And when it pops up, it's not that it pops up with one-eighth the intensity as before — it just pops up one-eighth as often as before.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so if you were working with someone and that popped up, what would you suggest that they do?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: It depends on exactly how it's manifesting. If in particular it's the low self-esteem, one of the things I recommend is doing lots of metta practice, and in particular doing metta practice for themselves — metta, loving-kindness practice, in the form of, yeah, “it's a good thing if I'm happy,” as opposed to “I deserve to be happy,” right? But more recognizing: yeah, it's a good thing if I'm happy. Yeah, I like it when I'm happy. It'd be a really good thing if I were happy. And then for the “deserve” part, which is often what is behind this — “I don't deserve to be happy,” or “I'm a terrible person,” or something — is to do a meditation and simply list to yourself good things that you've done. You helped the old lady across the street the other day, you know, whatever it is. Trivial, but at least get your mind out of the negative space and into a positive space. So those are two of the things that are most useful for the low self-esteem when that comes up.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And would this typically be a replacement for the jhana practice for a while, or is it an addendum? How do you see that working?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: In general, it's a replacement, unless what comes up is pretty minor and can be addressed quite quickly. In other words, what comes up is probably the primary thing that's up right now, and until it's no longer primary, trying to work with jhana practice is going to be quite difficult. Now, how long will it take you to get it to where — all right, you didn't solve it completely, but it's not coming up as your distraction when you're meditating? For some people, yeah, maybe it's only a few hours. Some people, yeah, it's the rest of the retreat and another session with their psychotherapist and another retreat. Yeah, so it varies enormously as to the intensity with which it comes up, how strongly it continues to come up, et cetera.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's so interesting that — and in a way it's completely logical — that in order to get into this highly focused place with a still mind, we have to work out some of the turbulent material. So you could almost see this kind of material arising as not some kind of blocking of your jhana, but actually the real thing you're trying to do with your meditation in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly. Well put. My teacher would say a moment of concentration is a moment of purification. And so, yeah, bringing this stuff up is purification practice. It's not pleasant, but it's definitely a really powerful and positive thing to do. It's just not any fun.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so “purification” used in that way is sometimes confusing. I think the idea is that you're unknotting the tangledness of your psychology. Or how would you talk about that purification to an average Westerner? We don't tend to use the word that way, right?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. The simile from the suttas is a piece of cloth. And if your piece of cloth is really dirty and you try and dye it, you're going to have a mess. You know, the dye is not going to go in evenly or smooth or anything like that.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And if you wash it, the dye comes off with the dirt.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right, exactly. So you want a nice, clean piece of cloth that will accept the dye. All right? It will accept a different view, basically. All right, so most of what goes on in our minds is self-centered. We operate from a very egocentric perspective, and that egocentric perspective is primarily about protection, although there is a fair amount of wanting pleasure, right? So, greed and fear.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: So if we're coloring our mind with looking to be safe and trying to get some happiness, for me, we're going to have problems seeing what's actually going on. And if the tendencies, the habits of mind, the unresolved trauma is popping up there, it's soiling the mind, so that the dye of reality can't come in there and actually color your mind so you can see what's actually happening. So I think that's the best analogy I can give you.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, so this wanting to be safe and also desiring pleasure of various sorts amounts to a kind of a bias.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And the idea is that this concentration practice is removing the bias over time.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Or straightening out the bias, at least temporarily, to be able to get into the jhanas.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: One of the prerequisites mentioned repeatedly in the suttas is the necessity of abandoning the five hindrances — the five hindrances being sense desire, anger and ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Or we could say pleasure-seeking, fear, too little energy, too much energy, and doubt.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: So the first two, the pleasure-seeking and the fear, are generally the ones that are coloring our minds as we go through our day, and we've got to set that aside. So it's necessary to set these aside long enough and strong enough to be able to get into these jhanic states. Getting into these jhanic states gives you a mind that, because of its indistractability, is less likely to fall back into those old pleasure-seeking, fear-running patterns. And while you're not falling into that, you're now looking at the world from a less egocentric perspective and have a much better chance of seeing what's actually happening.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: The idea behind seeing what's actually happening is: if you can operate in harmony with what's actually happening, rather than your desires and fears, your life is going to go much easier.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yes. And you may have deep insight into your own experience.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Oh, yes. This definitely happens along the way.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. So what do you see, besides the self-doubt or the negative self-talk coming up, that you wish you could just communicate to everyone who's trying to do jhanas all over the world? What's, like, the one thing that is just always apparent, that you wish you could just broadcast to the universe?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: I have to stop and think about it, because the self-doubt, low self-esteem is so huge. Looking for love in all the wrong places.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Looking for their pleasure in things that aren't going to give them satisfaction. Looking for safety in places that actually aren't going to be safe.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So, unwise action.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, unwise action. Action that actually isn't going to lead to the result that you're hoping for when you undertake the action. It's been quite interesting now that we have pictures into a huge number of people's minds with all of the interconnected, you know, Twitter and Facebook and everything else, and watch what people are up to and where they're trying to get their happiness and how they're trying to be safe. And yeah, this culture has failed miserably at actually providing sustainable sources of happiness and sustainable places of safety.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So is a big part of your work with people just helping them to be a little less damaging with their lives?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, though that's not my direct work. My direct work is: all right, here's how you can concentrate your mind. And then once they've got that down, here's how you can use your concentrated mind to investigate reality. And then the investigation of reality leads to, okay, here's how you can live your life in a less damaging fashion. But I don't go directly to that. It's more like I'm teaching technique. There are teachers out there who are almost anti-technique, and I'm very much technique-oriented. I mean, what we know from the Buddha — he had techniques and he was teaching them. And so I'm laying out the techniques that I have found helpful to me and saying, all right, try out these techniques and see if they're helpful for you.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay, so here we have someone. They're able to contact this piti-sukha that we were talking about for five to fifteen minutes. And now what?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Okay, so… that's the first jhana. All right, so you get to the first jhana. The first jhana is probably not the greatest place to hang out, because the piti can be a bit too agitating. Like I mentioned earlier, it might blow the top of your head off. So it could be too strong.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: What does that look like, having the piti be too strong?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: It generally tends to manifest physically as either vibration — okay, so you're just sitting there with this energy running through you that's causing you to vibrate — and/or as heat: you're getting basically a hot flash. All right? So it's actually uncomfortable.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's uncomfortable. It's so pleasant, it's not even pleasant.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah. All right? So the thing to do is to chill this down somewhat, move to a place that is less physical and more emotional, despite our differences discussing this. So you want to come from an agitated physical place with the piti predominating, to the piti being more in the background and the sukha, the joy-happiness, predominating. So now that you're focused on the experience of joy-happiness, however that manifests for you — that's the second jhana.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So it goes from piti-sukha to just sukha.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Sukha-piti.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Sukha being in the foreground, piti being in the background in the second jhana. Right. It says “with the subsiding of thinking and more thinking” — right, so the mind becomes much more collected — “and by gaining inner tranquility and unification of mind.” So things calm down mentally: inner tranquility, unification of mind. The mind focuses in more on the sukha-piti experience, is less likely to wobble, and you're really becoming absorbed into the joy-happiness experience with some background piti — you still got physical energy running in the background.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: And this is a much more sustainable place. The first jhana, if you've got it really strong, you may not want to be there more than 30 seconds. Anybody who's got it really strong tries to run it for 10 minutes — they're actually going to have negative effects when they get up.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: What do the negative effects look like?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Just agitated, just very agitated. The piti is still there. And if you do that before going to bed, you're not going to sleep. You come in to meditate the next sitting after you're doing this very agitated walking, and you're still agitated, you can't get settled. I mean, these are all possibilities, and it's just unpleasant. So if you get the first jhana really strong, you won't stay there long — you'll calm things down to get to the second. The second, you can stay there with no problem as long as you can maintain it. Now, these jhanic states are dependent on neurotransmitters, obviously, since all mental states are dependent on neurotransmitters. We don't know for sure what they are. I have my theories. My current theory is piti is dopamine breaking down into norepinephrine, and sukha is opioids.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Right. Now, you've only got a limited… endorphins.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Endorphins, yeah. You've only got a limited amount of that stuff, you know. It's not like you can generate it as fast as you can use it in these states. So for most people, they get in, say, to the second jhana, and they're running all these opioids and, yeah, just sort of the reservoir runs dry and it begins to tail off and get quiet.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Which is okay, because if you know what to do, you just simply ride that down into the third jhana, where the piti has gone away and the joy-happiness is now more contentment. Or you can, you know, hang out in the second jhana for a while and then intentionally move on to the third jhana, where the piti is gone. So now physically you're very quiet and still, and you're focused on the feeling of contentment.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And let's say someone was pretty good at doing the third jhana — would they run through the first and second one relatively quickly, only a few moments or a few minutes, and then straight into the third jhana? Is that the idea?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: I would say a few minutes, not moments. And I would say that on a retreat where you're doing multiple sitting meditation periods a day, occasionally you would want — at least the second jhana — you want to hang out in it for, you know, at least five minutes or so, right? Just give it time to get in there, and you get better skilled at it, as opposed to just always running on to the third. If someone learned the first four and, yeah, you get skilled at that, you're not going to stay long there. And this sitting, you spend five minutes in the second one and a little time in the third one, and then you hang out in four. Next time through, a little time in the first, a little time in the second, a little longer time in the third, you hang out in four. Next time through, you spend a lot of time in the second, a lot of time in the third, and it's less time in four. So you're varying it, so you keep your skill at each of these rather than just blasting through. This has two effects: one, your skill gets better; and two, staying longer in a jhana will enhance the next jhana. So if you run too fast through number two, you're going to have a weak three. So stay longer in two and let it build, and your three will be better.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, the difference between jhana one and jhana two is pretty clear, the way you described it. But the difference between two and three is not as clear in my mind yet.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: They are actually quite distinct. In two, there's a residual of piti, a residual of physical, energetic — we could even say agitation.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: You did say that, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: In the background. And in three, it's totally calm physically.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Right, okay.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: In the suttas it says of the third jhana, one experiences happiness with the body. And so the experience of happiness with the body in the third jhana is not so much due to the sukha — I mean, it does have its bodily component — but due to the tranquility of having exhausted the piti. You could think of the tranquility of the third jhana, the happiness with the body of the third jhana, much like a post-orgasmic glow. All right? So you get all this excited and agitated in the first and second, and now in the third you're in this afterglow of all that piti, and your mind is, yeah, really in a very contented space. You got a whole bunch of excitement, you don't need that anymore. All right, you fulfilled your dopamine craving.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: You've got nice opioids, and it's got you in a really nice contented place, and you're just happy to hang out there.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Good. So that's very clear. So here we are, glowing with endorphins or whatever. How do we then move into the fourth jhana?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Fourth jhana is described as a state beyond pleasure and pain. Well, the pleasure of that contentment is very obvious in the third. So the trick is simply let go of any pleasure in your mind. In the first jhana I've got a big grin — you can see my teeth. Second jhana, I got a big smile, no teeth. Third jhana, I got a wispy Buddha smile. All I have to do to go to the fourth is put my attention in the physical sensations of that wispy Buddha smile and then relax all the muscles in my face. When I do, there's a sense of things starting to drop down, and I just shift my attention to this feeling of dropping down and go with it, and let it settle into a place of quiet stillness, which turns out to be emotionally neutral. Nothing positive, nothing negative. That's the fourth jhana.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And where would your attention be at that moment?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: On the quiet stillness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And where is that located?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, you still want it embodied someplace.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I didn't say it had to be in the body. I just am asking, where is it?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: You don't have to have a “where” in order to focus on it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, true.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Okay? So if I told you where it was for me, it might be somewhere else for you. So it really isn't a useful piece of information. It's wherever you find it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay. Are you going to find it looking outside anywhere?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: When you're in the fourth jhana, you're going to feel like you're quite cocooned. You might find the front of the cocoon is maybe a foot in front of your face, and it comes up pretty much almost touching your back, and you're in this sort of egg-shaped cocoon there. And you're going to find the quiet stillness within that cocoon. Now, whether it's in front of you or inside of you, it just depends on how it manifests. I've spent a lot of time having people describe how they are experiencing each of these jhanas, and the little aids and whatnot that they find are helpful for them to know where to put their mind exactly. Some people see colors with the jhanas. Some people want to associate the four jhanas with the four seasons. I mean, you get all sorts of stuff like this happening. And it's like, okay, whatever helps you find and maintain these states is fine. It is where you find it, and it doesn't really matter.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And so do you find that people want to hang out in this fourth jhana state basically forever?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, you often hear something from Western teachers about, yeah, you can get addicted to the jhanas. And yeah, people can become jhana junkies. Ayya Khema said, would you rather live in a neighborhood full of heroin junkies or jhana junkies?

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: You just used a name there.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Ayya Khema was my teacher.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Oh, so Ayya Khema said this.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. Yeah, she was very serious and she had a great sense of humor. So, yeah, my job as a teacher is to keep an eye on the students. Once they've learned the fourth jhana, I say something like, okay, what sort of insight practice are you going to be working on? Or, I think you should work on this as an insight practice. And okay, now go away and work on the fourth jhana and then practice your insight practice. And if they come back and all they did was fourth jhana and didn't do their insight practice, then I'm going to come down hard on them. But most people, you know, they sort of grudgingly go play with an insight practice. And when they suddenly get the flood of insights, like they never got from that practice before, then the jhana junkie is cured. Because the insights are actually far more interesting than just getting high and hanging out.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: This is the central insight of the Buddha, correct? That these jhanas are incredibly powerful as a, let's say, setup and purification and preparation, and they are intrinsically pleasant, and yet they're really the doorway to do the insight practice. Is that how you would describe it?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, I've referred to the jhanas as a warm-up exercise. Now, they do have their own intrinsic usefulness, right? So now you begin to learn that, oh yeah, there's positive mental states inside of me that don't require an external trigger. And that's kind of a useful thing to know, so you don't go looking in all the wrong places. So in that sense, there's that insight from hanging out in these states. Hanging out in these states does change you.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Neuroscience has found that whatever mental states you tend to hang out in — well, that's going to become your default. And it's possible to move your emotional default more towards the positive if you just go hang out in more positive states. And the first four jhanas are obviously very positive states, so hanging out in them is going to make you a happier person. Of course, that's probably a long-term project — you'd have to practice pretty seriously for five years before you start noticing anything like that. And you probably can't determine, oh yeah, the fact that I'm happier now is 23% due to the jhanas and 64% due to the insight. I mean, that's not going to be possible. But I think long-term, yeah, the benefits of just doing jhana practice are going to make you at least somewhat happier. So there are other things other than them just being a warm-up exercise for insight, but I would say the warm-up exercise for insight is the best part of practicing them.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Jhanas are so powerful and beautiful. I'm always surprised how often bringing them up elicits a negative response from other meditators.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah. There's a lot of misinformation out there — a lot of topics, but this one in particular. I think part of it is competitiveness. You know: I've got a practice, I don't do jhanas, I'm doing fine, what are you trying to push on me? You know, don't say that you're better than me because you do jhanas. I mean, you know, this sort of thing comes up.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: The meditative competitiveness.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. I think that's one of it. Two, these people may have been cautioned against them by their misguided teachers. You know, when the hippies went to Asia and began studying with the teachers over there, those teachers weren't going to try to teach them Visuddhimagga jhanas, which is basically the Theravadan understanding of the jhanas — because, I mean, even the Asian monks couldn't do them for the most part, so these hippies, they don't have a chance. So they poo-pooed them, and the teachers come back and poo-poo them as well. So there's a lot of poo-poohing of jhanas. So people who are opposed to them may have heard their teachers poo-poohing them, and they take that on as part of what's going on.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, this is what you typically hear: oh, you're going to get stuck in the jhana, or, as you said, you're going to become addicted, and they're not intrinsically awakening.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. They're not intrinsically awakening. And… if you want to go to Muir Woods from Oakland, the Richmond–San Rafael Bridge is not Muir Woods, but it's actually a very useful thing to have along the way. Otherwise, you're going to need to swim across the bay. The road to the Grand Canyon is not the Grand Canyon, but without the road it's going to be a lot harder to get there. They are not awakening, but they are certainly a useful tool along the road to awakening. And yeah, like I say, there's a lot of misinformation out there, and it's really a shame. I mean, I do what I can to try and correct that.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: If people would listen to me, they'd have a much happier life, but a lot of people just don't pay attention. I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Exactly. That's why we're doing this podcast.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So we've talked about four jhanas, and yet in most lists there are eight jhanas, the second four being the immaterial jhanas. How do we approach these immaterial jhanas? What does it even mean to be immaterial?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Okay, so that's the designation that they were given, right? In the sense that there's no bodily awareness. So they are arupa.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay. Rupa…

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Without form.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Without form.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. So the first four are called the rupa jhanas, the material jhanas — not because they are material, but because there is bodily awareness in each of these. It says that one drenches, steeps, saturates, and suffuses one's body with the piti and sukha, or whatever the object is. So in order to drench, steep, saturate, suffuse your body, you need to have bodily awareness.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, you're saying that list really fast. What is it?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Drench, steep, saturate, and suffuse. This is a typical thing you find in Pali to emphasize something — they throw a lot of very similar-meaning words together. In fact, the words vitakka and vicara actually just mean thinking and more thinking, not initial and sustained attention. That only shows up in the commentaries and later. Okay? It's just emphasizing: oh, there's thinking in the first jhana, and it gets quiet in the second when that goes away.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay, so “drench, steep, saturate, and suffuse” just means fill your body with the piti-sukha experience. In the first jhana?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: In the first and second, and then the third with the sukha experience, and then the fourth with the quiet stillness, right? “The pure bright mind” is actually what it says.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Okay, but we could say the quiet stillness.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: The instructions for the fifth jhana, the first immaterial, is “by passing entirely beyond all bodily sensations.” So right off, you need to have a level of concentration where you're no longer aware of bodily sensations. So in order to get to these higher jhanas, you need a really good fourth jhana. So you've got to get skilled at the first four before you're ready to tackle the higher ones. But if you manage to get to the fifth and higher, then, as I mentioned earlier, your concentration level goes up quite noticeably. The objects there are almost visualizations. But it's not like — if I say to you now, visualize a candle.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: And you can probably get some sort of thing in your mind, right? And you intentionally did that. But these are not… when it says visualize infinite space — no, that's not what happens.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: The fifth one is called the realm of infinite space, or actually the realm of limitless space. And it's an experience that you have that, if you go to describe it, you would say, I was seeing or sensing this limitless space. So if you're visual, it will appear visually to you. But you get there by focusing on outward expansion. Basically, get a good fourth jhana and then find something you can expand without limit. My teacher came and said, expand your body without limit. It doesn't matter what you expand. I had a student expand — blow up a balloon, right, and follow it. Whatever you expand without limit, stay focused on the edges of that expansion, and then — pop! — vast infinite space appears before you.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Don't look for the space. If you look for the space, you're not focused on the expansion, and it won't happen. If you just stay with the expansion, out on the edges, out to infinity, then this vast space suddenly pops into being. And if you're visual, you see it. If you're not visual, you'll know it's there. Because I'm visual and see it, I can't really tell you how the people who aren't visual experience it. But yeah, this sense of a vast space. It's almost a visualization, but it's not you intentionally trying to visualize vast space. It just pops in once you get your mind expanded far enough.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: The sixth one is the realm of infinite consciousness. And it's a shift from the space to your consciousness of that space. Your consciousness has to be as big as that space, right, if you're going to experience it. And so your consciousness has to be infinite. And so it's a subtle shift. It's more like you go from experiencing the space before you to getting absorbed into the space and being aware of your consciousness of space. Your consciousness becomes infinite. Your mind becomes infinite.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: The seventh is the realm of no-thingness. This is the one that the Buddha learned from his first teacher. And the trick there is to shift your attention from the consciousness to the content of that consciousness, which turns out to be nothing. There is no content. The sense of space is long gone. And so now, can you find a sense of nothing and just focus on it? It's kind of a small nothing at first, but if you stay with it, it gets to be a big nothing. You look at it, there it is, and you look towards the edge, and there's nothing over towards where you thought the edge was. And then you look at the other, and there's nothing over there, and it's a big nothing. Usually dark.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: People who stumble into this state by accident usually freak out. They feel they've fallen into the void. Nope, they've just fallen into the seventh jhana. I've had a number of students report falling in, usually on the three-month course at IMS or something like that, where they had a lot of time to meditate. And then when they come back there intentionally, it's like, oh yeah, this is right where I was. Only it wasn't scary this time. What was scary was fear of the unknown. What's happened to me? Well, I'm in a big, dark room.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Right. That's already scary.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah. A real big dark room, and there are no walls.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: And then the eighth is called the realm of neither perception nor non-perception. And, well, it's a state that has no characteristics by which you can describe it. So it makes it very difficult for me to talk about it, other than to say that it's a state that has no characteristics by which you can describe it. But you know that you're in a state that has no characteristics by which you can describe it. And it's also much more fragile than the other ones. And this is what the Buddha learned from his second teacher.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So that is, of course, an intriguing and confusing non-definition.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah. The good news about the eighth is if you get good at the seventh, it's fairly easy to find the eighth. It's not hard to find it — it's hard to stay there, because it is so subtle. I practiced for almost a year, and then was on a month-long retreat, before I ever got into eight when I wanted and stayed for about half an hour. And I'd gotten that skill with all the others much, much, much quicker.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And then I've seen lists that include a ninth jhana.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Ninth jhana is spoken of in the suttas. It's referred to as the cessation of feeling and perception.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, is this nirodha samapatti, or something different than that?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yes. It goes by lots of names: ninth jhana, cessation of perception and feeling, nirodha samapatti — number nine. So it gets a lot of different names, but it's a state of suspended animation. You might have heard about, you know, these Indian mystics — they put them in a coffin, bury them in the ground for a week, dig them up and they're fine. Yeah, so they put themselves into this state. It's actually possible to see someone go into this state in this great movie called Shortcut to Nirvana, which is a documentary on the Kumbh Mela festival that happened in, I believe it was 2000, 2001. There's a Japanese woman who climbs down into this pit that they've dug. They pulled the ladder out, they put roofing tin over, they cover it with dirt. The documentary goes on. Three days later, they come back, sweep off the dirt, put the ladder down. She climbs out all happy. She obviously put herself into that state to stay there for three days.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Lights out.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah, it's being unconscious. And interestingly enough, it appears that the first Visuddhimagga jhana is actually an entrance into this state. Because in the first Visuddhimagga jhana there's no bodily awareness, there's no hearing, no sounds, and there's no passage of time, which totally fits the description of nirodha.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And yet, if we're starting at nirodha, how could there be jhanas after that? We're already kind of completely shut down.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Well, according to Venerable Pa Auk, you can't tell where you were until you come out. And when you come out, if you look at your heart center, you can see a reflection of the factors of the jhana you were just in. Okay, and that's the best I can do, because I'm not a Pa Auk jhana practitioner.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, fascinating. A lot of people talk about weird experiences with the jhanas. Daniel Ingram was on the show and was talking quite a bit about strange manifestations with jhanic concentration. Not necessarily difficult states, but just weird stuff. And Shinzen talked about that as well. What's your experience with that?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: The most common thing is heightened sensory input afterwards. I can still see those pansies outside the meditation hall where I got good at jhana number eight. First time I had a really good eighth jhana, I walk outside and I look at those pansies and they're, you know, burned into my mind. So yeah, there's a very definite heightened sensory awareness. Colors are much more vivid and sounds are more beautiful, you know, things like that. That's probably the most common thing that happens.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: There certainly have been numerous reports of people having enhanced ESP experiences post-jhana. Now, when I say ESP, extrasensory perception, I'm not claiming that it's a proven thing. What I'm saying is there certainly is an experience that people have that they want to label with ESP. And whatever those experiences are — whether it's real, genuine, scientifically not yet discovered telepathy, or it's just people picking up subtle cues, or wishful thinking, or whatever it is — that definitely gets enhanced by strong concentration.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So, I mean, this is even talked about in the suttas. There are two of the supernormal powers that are described that include knowing the minds of others and hearing sounds at a distance. And these are both common ESP experiences, whatever they are. And in fact, the suttas have a whole list of what we might call magical powers or superpowers that one gains by doing the jhanas. So is that something that you've tried, or you find interesting at all?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: I definitely found it interesting. I would put them into three categories, this list. The first thing is the mind-made body. And it says, from this body one creates another body, complete in all its form, defective in no parts — which of course is, yeah, right. What? Huh? Okay, let's set that one aside. The next is the magical powers: walking on water, flying through the air, being one becoming many, being many becoming one, appearing and disappearing, et cetera.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So, Matrix-type experiences.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Yeah. And so I was talking with a friend of mine when I was teaching in Portugal who's into lucid dreaming. And he mentioned that it's possible to go directly from a waking state into a lucid dream. It's called wake-induced lucid dreaming — WILD. So, of course, I asked Mr. Google about that. And the state you need to get yourself into in order to go from waking into WILD is just like what you have coming out of the fourth jhana. So I'm saying that learning to make a mind-made body is learning the wake-induced lucid dreaming technique. And what do you do in a lucid dream? Oh, how about fly through the air, walk on water, et cetera, et cetera. So I'm claiming that those are actually lucid dreams. Extremely vivid, seemingly realistic. And you've got control.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: There's a sutta that backs that up. It's in the Numerical Discourses 3.60. And in that, the Buddha and a brahmin are having a conversation, and the brahmin says that these magical powers only benefit the one who does them. And the Buddha agrees.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So it sounds like it's a private experience.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: One assumes it's not happening in objective reality at that point, to us modern Westerners.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I'm curious, though — they do use that phrase, that it's helpful or useful to the doer of them. And so have you found these to be useful, or do you see them actually having a positive effect?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Well, those in particular — the only walking on water I ever did was one time in Sweden in the winter.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's really easy. Yeah, somehow we can all do that one.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right, exactly. So no, I haven't found that particularly useful, other than to say that when one begins to realize what the mind can manufacture out of nothing, then you maybe pay a little more careful attention to actually picking up what's actually happening, as opposed to your wishful thinking and so forth. So in the sense that one begins to step beyond believing everything that runs through your mind, then that can be very helpful. But other than that, I can't really say. So that's the first two. The next two we talked about — the knowing the minds of others and hearing sounds at a distance — that's ESP, whatever ESP is.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Might be more lucid dreaming.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Might be more lucid dreaming. I'm guessing it's whatever the average person in the San Francisco Bay Area is experiencing when they say they have ESP experiences. And we don't know whether that's scientific or wishful thinking or anything in between.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. Okay.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: And the last two are usually given as remembering past lives, and seeing beings passing away and re-arising according to their karma. What Stephen Batchelor had to say was basically that in a culture that's steeped in multiple lifetimes, these two are phrased in such a way that would really appeal to the depths of understanding that actions have consequences. In other words, they weren't meant to be taken literally. But the first one is personal: I am the result of a lot of past actions that I have done. And the second one: everybody reaps what they sow. And that that's what's going on there.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: We could go into quite a long discussion of those two if you wanted to, but maybe we could save that for some other time.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Maybe another one.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So these immaterial jhanas are, of course, quite powerful and fascinating, and yet what I understand you to be saying is they're not actually necessary levels for charging your insight practice up to the level where it can be truly awakening.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Right. It would appear that it would be good if you can actually get to the first jhana, to practice them well enough to get to the fourth. That's fairly doable. Not everybody, but a lot of people, given enough time, enough retreats, can get to the first four. If you can do five through eight, or even just five, then you're going to have a deeper level of concentration. But it doesn't appear that it's necessary, that coming out of four you have deep enough concentration. Now, there is a sutta that indicates even coming out of the first jhana is sufficient. Though I personally find coming out of the first jhana is too much agitation for it to be that useful. But you're still pretty concentrated. Yeah, you're more concentrated than you were at access concentration, so you get a boost right there. But if you can't get to the jhanas — almost everybody can get to access concentration. So even if you're not a jhana practitioner, get to access concentration and then do your vipassana practice. That will enhance your vipassana practice quite a bit.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: A lot of people listening are having a family, having house payments, and so on. Are jhanas practical for someone who is not going on long retreats, or are they very retreat-dependent?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: For almost everyone, it requires you to go on a retreat to learn the jhanas. It requires that you have a good daily practice before going on that retreat, and it requires you have a good daily practice to keep them, to take the jhanas home from that retreat. So yeah, your spiritual practice has to be a pretty high priority in your life for this to work. But it is possible to go on a retreat, learn the jhanas, and bring them home and keep them for, let's say, some period of time.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Dependent upon, one, how well you learn them in the retreat, how well you know exactly what to do and what they feel like; and two, how good is your daily practice. If your daily practice is an hour in the morning, an hour in the evening, every day — yeah, no problem, you can keep it just like you had on the retreat. If it's an hour once a day, yeah, you keep it for quite a while. If it's 45 minutes five days a week, yeah, you might keep them for a few months. If it's once a week for 45 minutes — nah, they're gone.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So what's coming up for me is I just want to come back to the importance of the jhanas. How are they important for someone who wants to meditate or has a powerful meditation practice? Why should I care about the jhanas?

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: They are a skill. Like all skills, they have to be learned and practiced. They are a skill that, if you can develop some mastery, will enhance your spiritual practice and repay the effort you put into learning them and manifesting them. They'll pay quite big dividends.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Not everyone manages to learn the jhanas. They're not for everybody. If the jhanas required multitasking, I wouldn't be anywhere in the ballpark — I just can't multitask. But because I'm the opposite of a multitasker, I'm really good at doing one thing at a time, they came quite easily to me. So if you find that these states are accessible, they're well worth the time and effort, because the mind state you have coming out of these states is such that your investigation of reality is going to be definitely very enhanced. So they're optional on the spiritual path, but they're such a good option that if you can manage to manifest them, it's going to be very, very worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Thank you so much, Leigh. It's been great to talk to you today.

transcript.speaker: Leigh Brasington
transcript.text: Oh, my pleasure. I totally enjoyed talking on this subject. Thanks.
